This patient presents with classic “red flag” features of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI): acute periumbilical abdominal pain (often out of proportion to exam), hematochezia (suggesting mucosal or transmural infarction), and high-risk cardiovascular comorbidities — specifically a recent myocardial infarction (1 week prior), long-standing diabetes, and hypertension. These strongly favor an **embolic etiology**, as atrial fibrillation or left ventricular thrombus post-MI are common sources of mesenteric artery emboli. The epigastric bruit suggests underlying atherosclerotic stenosis (e.g., celiac or SMA origin), which may predispose to both embolic occlusion and low-flow ischemia during hypotensive episodes. Hypotension (95/65 mmHg) and tachycardia further support a component of **low-flow (non-occlusive) mesenteric ischemia**, especially in the setting of recent cardiac decompensation. CT angiography confirming reduced mesenteric arterial flow is diagnostic — it differentiates AMI from other causes of hematochezia (e.g., diverticulosis, IBD, infectious colitis) and excludes mechanical obstruction or primary colonic pathology. The absence of overt peritoneal signs does not mitigate concern; AMI frequently presents with subtle or delayed physical findings, and progression to infarction and perforation can occur rapidly. All evidence converges on a life-threatening, time-sensitive diagnosis requiring immediate revascularization.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute mesenteric ischemia

[THOUGHT]  
This patient presents with classic “red flag” features of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI): acute periumbilical abdominal pain (often out of proportion to exam), hematochezia (suggesting mucosal or transmural infarction), and high-risk cardiovascular comorbidities — specifically a recent myocardial infarction (1 week prior), long-standing diabetes, and hypertension. These strongly favor an **embolic etiology**, as atrial fibrillation or left ventricular thrombus post-MI are common sources of mesenteric artery emboli. The epigastric bruit suggests underlying atherosclerotic stenosis (e.g., celiac or SMA origin), which may predispose to both embolic occlusion and low-flow ischemia during hypotensive episodes. Hypotension (95/65 mmHg) and tachycardia further support a component of **low-flow (non-occlusive) mesenteric ischemia**, especially in the setting of recent cardiac decompensation. CT angiography confirming reduced mesenteric arterial flow is diagnostic — it differentiates AMI from other causes of hematochezia (e.g., diverticulosis, IBD, infectious colitis) and excludes mechanical obstruction or primary colonic pathology. Hematochezia in this context is not due to benign anorectal bleeding but rather ischemic injury to the distal small bowel or right colon — territories commonly supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. The absence of overt peritoneal signs does not mitigate concern; AMI frequently presents with subtle or delayed physical findings, and progression to infarction and perforation can occur rapidly. All evidence converges on a life-threatening, time-sensitive diagnosis requiring immediate revascularization.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute mesenteric ischemia
